stem:
At 50 hours, a well term baby is due for newborn bloodspot screening. The parents ask to skip it: the newborn examination was normal, nobody in either family has an inherited condition, and the baby is feeding well.

What best explains why the test still matters?

options.label: A
options.text: Screened conditions are silent at birth and treatable before harm
options.explanation: Conditions such as congenital hypothyroidism, phenylketonuria and cystic fibrosis usually look normal at birth, and early treatment prevents harm. That is why every well baby is screened.

options.label: B
options.text: It completes the check for chromosome conditions missed antenatally
options.explanation: Bloodspot screening targets selected metabolic, endocrine and other conditions, not chromosome conditions in general.

options.label: C
options.text: It excludes the inherited conditions the family history did not cover
options.explanation: Most babies with a screened condition have no family history, and screening identifies higher risk rather than excluding every inherited condition.

options.label: D
options.text: It records a baseline in case the baby becomes unwell in the first year
options.explanation: The card is stored, but the test exists to screen for specific treatable conditions, not to provide a baseline for later illness.

options.label: E
options.text: It detects conditions that the newborn examination should have found
options.explanation: The screened conditions usually cannot be found on examination at birth; a normal examination is exactly why the test is needed.

context: Newborn bloodspot screening finds selected serious conditions that look normal at birth and are treatable before harm, so a normal examination or family history is no reason to skip it.
